issues.description: The length of the 'suicide attempt episode' is defined inconsistently across the manuscript. The Methods state the attempt episode is the one-week period before the attempt, but the abstract, hypotheses, and analyses describe a two-week (14-day) window. This is a fundamental inconsistency in the central predictor/window and undermines replicability and interpretation of which data were actually analyzed.
issues.quote: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation

issues.description: The authors repeatedly characterize a fundamentally retrospective design (participants recall past episodes and dates) as 'prospective.' Although the text data accrued in real time, episode identification, classification, and timeline reconstruction were entirely retrospective. Labeling this as a prospective design overstates the inferential strength and confuses readers about the actual evidentiary basis.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a ‘true’ prospective study design.

issues.description: The analysis window was partly chosen by visually inspecting the data for where change appeared most pronounced, then significance tests for temporal change were run on those same data. Using the outcome data to select the analysis window before testing introduces circularity and inflates the chance of finding significant temporal effects (a 'garden of forking paths' problem).
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced... changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.description: The p-value for the sad-words episode-type effect is reported as p=.003 in the Results text but as p=.033 in Table 2 (with the same chi-square = 8.74). These differ by an order of magnitude and one crosses interpretive thresholds differently, raising concerns about accuracy of reported statistics.
issues.quote: Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003.

issues.description: The text states desire to die 'significantly decreased' from pre to post, but the reported means show an INCREASE (0.82 to 1.03), and Table 1 lists a change of +0.20. A statistically significant increase in desire to die over the study session is a potential iatrogenic effect that is mislabeled as a decrease, which both misstates the data and obscures a possible safety concern.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.

issues.description: It is stated that all 27 participants with SMS data had data from at least one reported suicide attempt, which implies at least 27 attempt episodes with SMS data, yet only 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data are reported. These figures cannot both be correct and the true number of attempt episodes contributing to analyses is unclear.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt... Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data, the most common methods

issues.subcategory: random effects structure / Type I error control
issues.description: The authors claim a maximal random-effects structure was used to protect against inflated Type I error, but for the key temporal (Analysis 2) models the full random-slope models failed to converge and NO random slopes were included. Omitting by-participant random slopes for the interaction of interest is known to substantially inflate Type I error for exactly the interaction effects being interpreted, contradicting the stated rationale and threatening the validity of the significant slope findings.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.description: The Discussion asserts that the high-risk period was associated with greater anxiety, but in Primary Analysis 1 anxiety was non-significant (chi-square=3.62, p=.306). Only sad words reached significance (and not uniquely). Claiming an anxiety effect overstates the findings.
issues.quote: few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.description: Analyses are conducted at the individual-message level (189,478 messages) from only 27 participants and ~134 episodes. Even with random intercepts, modeling at the message level can yield extremely high effective power and produce 'significant' but trivially small effects (note tiny betas, e.g., 0.010-0.027) that may be driven by differences in message volume rather than meaningful psychological change. This undermines interpretation of the significant slope effects.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.description: A large number of tests were run across many LIWC variables, episode-type contrasts, and means vs. slopes, with no correction for multiple comparisons. Many of the reported 'significant' effects are at borderline p-values (e.g., p=.049, .046, .046, .049, .011), making it likely that some are false positives. While the authors justify not correcting, in an underpowered exploratory pilot this substantially weakens confidence in the positive findings.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.description: Although described as within-subjects, the compared episodes occurred at different (potentially years-apart) points in participants' lives, with different phones, relationships, developmental stages, and life circumstances. Differences in language across episode types may reflect these temporal/contextual confounds rather than suicide-risk state, yet this is not addressed as a confound.
issues.quote: We analyzed and compared text messages during episodes within person based on a number of features selected a priori

issues.description: LIWC was designed and validated primarily on longer prose. Applying percentage-based LIWC categories to very short SMS messages produces highly unstable scores (a single word in a short text yields large percentage swings), and the authors themselves note negation problems. The reliability/validity of LIWC for short text messages is not established or addressed.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.description: The sample is a small convenience sample drawn from a university subject pool (mean age 20.4, 84.8% female, predominantly college students), with predominantly non-injurious 'attempts.' Because males are roughly four times more likely to die by suicide and the sample is young and female-dominated, generalizability to the broader at-risk and suicide-decedent population is severely limited, beyond what the authors acknowledge.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: The 'suicide attempt' outcome includes aborted/interrupted incidents where no physical action occurred (71% caused no physical harm; e.g., driving to a bridge but not jumping). Combining these with actual attempts conflates heterogeneous states and weakens the validity of the 'high risk / attempt' category that anchors all analyses.
issues.quote: 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm (e.g., driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump)

issues.description: The power analysis is anchored on large between-subjects effect sizes from prior literature, yet the study uses a within-subjects design for which the authors concede the effect sizes are unknown and may differ substantially. Basing the power justification on potentially inapplicable effect sizes, and concluding only large effects are detectable, leaves the study's sensitivity poorly characterized.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis based on the assumption of large effect sizes (though no prior studies have examined within-subjects differences, which may or may not vary substantially from between-subjects comparisons)

issues.description: Throughout, the manuscript frames retrospective, within-subject correlational findings as 'real-time digital biomarkers,' 'predictors of suicidal behaviors,' and tools to identify imminent risk 'in real time.' The design cannot establish predictive or temporal-forecasting validity; these claims substantially overstate what the data support.
issues.quote: This laboratory investigation identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors, which may be utilized in the future by machine learning models to predict acute suicide risk

issues.description: Only 134 of 293 episodes (46%) had SMS data, and iPhone encryption and missing backups systematically excluded data. Which episodes had retrievable data is likely nonrandom (e.g., more recent episodes, certain device types), introducing selection bias that could correlate with episode type and recency, biasing comparisons.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: Episode dates and types relied on single-informant retrospective self-report, and the authors note 90.3% certainty (meaning ~10% uncertain, possibly off by days). Given that the critical effects are day-level slopes over a ~14-day window, even small dating errors could materially distort temporal trajectories, a threat not fully reconciled with the day-resolution analyses.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.description: Time (day -14 to 0) is modeled as a single linear slope and interpreted as steady escalation, yet the authors' own visual inspection suggested change concentrated around 7 days. A linear day term may misrepresent nonlinear trajectories, and the chosen specification is not justified or compared to alternatives.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0), and the interaction of episode type and day

issues.description: For anger, the omnibus interaction is only marginal (chi-square=7.83, p=.049) yet all three pairwise contrasts are reported as significant (p=.046, .013, .011), and positive emotion's attempt-vs-ideation contrast is borderline (p=.049). The reliance on numerous just-under-.05 results in an admittedly underpowered pilot, combined with the missing random-slope correction, makes these key findings statistically fragile.
issues.quote: anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=2.00, p=.046), depressed (z=2.49, p=.013), and positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes

issues.description: Some key inferential statistics are not reported in the text (e.g., the omnibus chi-square for the anger interaction is described as 'significant' without the value in text), and effect sizes are reported only as log-odds betas (which are tiny, e.g., 0.004-0.027) without a clear interpretable magnitude. This hampers assessment of the practical significance of findings.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt

issues.description: The 'emotional tone' (Tone) measure is a proprietary, non-transparent LIWC algorithm, yet it is treated as a continuous outcome and one of the highlighted significant effects (vs depressed, p<.001). Reliance on a black-box composite limits interpretability and reproducibility of this finding.
issues.quote: several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.description: Participants contributed on average only ~1.5 episodes per type, and many did not provide all four episode types, yielding highly unbalanced and sparse cells for a within-subjects contrast across four levels. This sparseness limits the robustness of within-subject episode-type comparisons regardless of the mixed-model framework.
issues.quote: Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type.

issues.description: The introduction asserts a model 'accounted for 80.3% of the variance' to characterize risk-factor research as 'impressive,' which conflates variance explained in some outcome with imminent-risk prediction and is potentially a misleading citation; combined with strong claims of being the 'first study' to analyze private SMS, the framing overstates both prior capability and the present contribution.
issues.quote: a recent model, which included known risk factors for suicide attempt, accounted for 80.3% of the variance (Nock, Borges, & Ono, 2012).

issues.description: Several outcomes (e.g., emotional tone, ratios of sent/received words) are bounded or ratio variables that were analyzed with linear mixed models assuming normally distributed residuals. Ratios and bounded percentage scores often violate LMM assumptions, and no diagnostics or justification for distributional appropriateness are provided for these specific outcomes.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM)
